title: Influence of Si and Al on the Mechanical Properties of Advanced High-Strength Steels (AHSS) in the As-Cast State
abstract: Abstract Developments in third-generation advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) have produced stronger and more formable steels for the automotive industry by controlling chemical composition and mechanical processing. Cracking during cooling after continuous casting has been a prominent problem for these steels and is believed to be influenced by the steel microstructures. In this study, the effects of chemical composition on the mechanical properties are investigated for as-cast steels by performing mechanical tests on steels containing 0.2 wt pct C and 3 wt pct Mn with varying Si and Al concentrations up to 3 wt pct. Tensile tests were performed to measure strength and ductility at temperatures from 200 °C to 600 °C. Si-alloyed steels have the highest yield strength, while combined silicon- and aluminum-alloyed steels have higher ductility. Fracture surfaces were examined and crack paths were found not to propagate along the ferrite in the microstructure.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Third-generation advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) are being developed to meet the automotive industry’s demands of stronger and more formable steel. These steels are highly alloyed resulting in complex microstructures which influence the mechanical properties significantly. These grades are also known to have defects and cracking tendencies during solidification and cooling which can lead to slab fracture. [ 1 ]

A recent investigation into steels containing 0.2 pct C and 3 pct Mn, with different additions of Si and Al, has shown that different chemical compositions lead to microstructures with two ferrite morphologies—proeutectoid and primary ferrite. [ 2 ]  Proeutectoid ferrite is common in individual Si-alloyed steels, while primary ferrite is common in high addition Si + Al steels as well as 2 pct Al steel. This paper investigates the mechanical properties of these steels, including the fracture behavior and fracture path.

Understanding the different tensile failure mechanisms—brittle or ductile—aids understanding of how these alloys crack at different temperatures. Brittle fracture includes cleavage and intergranular fracture. [ 3 , 4 ]  A basic cracking process for cleavage fracture seen in most ferritic steels as proposed by Lin  et al. [ 5 ]  involves three steps: (1) a microcrack initiates at a carbide particle that meets both the nucleation and propagation requirements, (2) microcracks which form at the carbide/matrix interface then propagate along the (100) plane and (3) crack propagation across the first matrix grain boundary (ferrite/ferrite interface cracking). The limiting step depends on temperature. For bainitic steels, step (3) can be cracking within a bainite packet to the adjacent grains. [ 6 ,  7 – 8 ]

Other researchers [ 6 ]  have also proposed similar cleavage fracture processes involving crack initiation at a brittle particle, near martensite–austenite or particle–matrix interfaces in HSLA steels, as well as microcrack or void nucleation. All of these processes are considered valid for the steels studied in this paper.

Due to the number of carbides present in these steels, some more detail of the basic cleavage fracture process proposed by Lin et al [ 5 ]  is summarized here. Step (1) in the cracking process involves nucleation at the carbide particles along with some ferrite deformation. [ 5 ]  It is implied that for crack nucleation to occur, the particle sizes must be greater than 0.1 to 1  μ m. [ 3 ]  However, not all crack nucleation requires ferrite deformation. Crack propagation within the carbide particles would not trigger plastic deformation within the ferrite matrix and this is known as dynamic crack propagation. This crack can extend across the interface if its stress is greater than the carbide particle strength. It is concluded that the first carbide that meets both the nucleation and propagation requirements serves as a vital crack initiation point. [ 5 ]

Ferrite/ferrite interface cracking is dependent on the temperature. As temperature increases, the critical strain energy release rate of the ferrite/ferrite interface increases rapidly and is predicted to be greater than that of the carbide/ferrite interface. Continuation of the crack across the ferrite/ferrite interface happens when the stress surpasses the ferrite grain strength. When the ferrite grain strength is lower than the carbide particle strength, an unstable fracture path occurs after particle cracking. Conversely, if the ferrite grain strength is greater than that of the carbide particle, stable cleavage fracture and grain-sized cracks would be observed. [ 5 ]

The second common type of brittle fracture is intergranular. It is typically seen when impurities (elements such as P or S) segregate to the grain boundaries. [ 4 ]  Apart from impurity segregation, other factors that can influence intergranular cracks include the grain boundary orientation in relation to the stress axis and the structure of the grain boundaries. It is found that some structures are more susceptible to fracture than others which can be governed by the misorientation between the different grains. [ 8 , 9 ]

In ferritic steels, fracture of second-phase particles on grain boundaries can play a significant role in intergranular fracture. As the precipitation of carbide particles at the grain boundaries increases, intergranular fracture becomes more likely. Yet, it is noted that carbide particles must be accompanied by other impurities to cause brittle failure at the carbides. [ 9 ]

Apart from brittle fracture, ductile fracture is the most common failure mechanism in metals. The mechanisms of ductile fracture are governed by the nucleation, growth, and coalescence of voids. In high-strength alloys, this process occurs rapidly which results in very low ductility for some cases. [ 3 , 10 ]

Void formation or nucleation typically occurs at second-phase particles which are usually inclusions or carbide particles in these steels. [ 3 ]  After nucleation, these voids would grow and eventually coalesce, where a crack forms and the material fractures. [ 3 ]  Typically, uniform void growth is observed. However, for the alloys with a mixture of hard/soft matrix such as ferrite/martensite matrix, non-uniform void growth is observed. This phenomenon is also observed during void nucleation, where different inclusion sizes can influence the void formation. The interaction of different void sizes can result in different void growth rates which lead to larger-sized voids outgrowing the smaller ones. [ 11 , 12 ]

For smaller voids that grow among the larger ones, it is found that after the specimen reaches the maximum stress point the smaller voids grow more rapidly compared to the larger ones. [ 13 ]  The stress increase between the larger voids is smaller at larger void spacing. [ 11 ]

As shown later, non-uniform void growth (bimodal voids) was commonly observed in the steels of this study. Melander and Stahlberg tested different relationships between bimodal void sizes and populations, and ductility. Several conclusions were made from the study [ 14 ] : Material with a bimodal void distribution is more ductile than one with uniform voids The ductility increases as the distance between the two different sized voids increases Smaller voids only influence the overall ductility if the small voids have a similar or greater density than the larger voids Larger void width-to-height ratios generally increase the ductility

Temperature can also influence void nucleation and growth. At low temperatures, plasticity controls cavitation, whereas at high temperatures vacancy diffusion controls void growth. [ 14 , 15 ]  An investigation by Gernstein supported this finding as microscopic images of a dual-phase (DP) steel showed that at elevated temperatures, there is an increase in the void sizes as well as the number of large voids. It is also noted that at these temperatures, voids are reported to be rounder in shape as vacancy diffusion dominates. [ 16 ]

In various 3rd-generation AHSS grades, the fracture behavior was studied extensively in steels like DP or transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) steels. Some detrimental cracking mechanisms that occur in DP steels include ferrite–ferrite grain boundary fracture due to localized strain, detachment at the ferrite–martensite phase boundary due to the soft ferrite and hard martensite matrix, cracking inside the martensite, and delamination of the inclusions from the matrix. There are various factors that can influence the crack behavior of these steels but the most prominent causes stem from chemical composition and microstructural features. [ 17 , 18 ]

In Liu  et al. ’s [ 18 ]  study of the fracture behavior of DP1000 under different testing conditions, it is found that ductile failure is the predominant mechanism, where microvoids nucleation and coalescence eventually led to the macroscopic failure of the material. The voids identified for all fracture surfaces were homogeneous with some large voids. As the loading rates increase, shear bands appear instead of voids indicating that void growth is limited. From observing the fracture microstructure, cracking inside the martensite and debonding at the ferrite–martensite matrix were noticed where the former case caused shear fracture, while the latter resulted in microvoids formation. Other cracking features of DP steels also involve the martensite volume fraction, where martensite volume fraction exceeding 70 pct is the primary cracking mechanism in the steel. [ 19 ]

Apart from the ductile failure that is well known in DP steels, transgranular cleavage cracking was observed by Varanasi  et al . [ 17 ]  It is mentioned that the transgranular crack path observed is non-linear. Instead, zigzag lines were observed to propagate across the martensite. From EBSD images sampled from the fractured specimens, the cleavage planes identified were {110} and {112}. However, it was pointed out that the {100} cleavage plane could not be ruled out as it correlates to the linear morphology cleavage crack and ferrite cleavage crack. Ferrite cleavage cracks observed in DP steels measured by Morooka  et al . [ 20 ]  showed that at 5 pct applied strain, the martensite stress was greater than the ferrite stress by almost 50 pct. This caused the crack to propagate into the ferrite, along the {100} cleavage plane.

Simulations carried out by Suzudo  et al . [ 21 ]  compared all three cleavage planes and found out that at lower temperatures, bcc metals are brittle and that the most common cleavage plane is {100}, where {110}, {112}, and {111} were not. In summary, the ferrite {100} cleavage crack is most commonly seen in bcc metals which could be affected by the martensite cracking or an increased stress localization that can propagate the crack. There are some instances where ductile failure occur in the ferrite and one instance that has been observed by Varanasi  et al . [ 17 ]  showed that the presence of manganese sulfide (MnS) and ferrite leads to void formation in the ferrite.

The motivation behind this research is based on the limited understanding of the microstructural influence on the mechanical properties of the as-cast AHSS. It is known that these AHSS slabs crack at around 400 °C during cooling after continuous casting, yet no fundamental mechanisms have been detailed for the cracking phenomenon. [ 2 ]  Based on prior research, it can be summarized that highly alloyed 3 rd -generation AHSS exhibit complex microstructures, where numerous factors can affect the cracking behavior of the steel. Previous work [ 22 ]  indicated that the crack path of Charpy tensile specimens follows along the ferrite films for a 3 wt pct Si sample at 400 °C, which suggested that microstructures could be one of the cracking mechanisms of AHSS slabs during cooling.

In a previous study, [ 2 ]  the microstructures of as-cast steels were observed and investigated. It was discovered that the Si-alloyed, Al-alloyed, and Si + Al alloyed steels have different types of microstructures, where proeutectoid ferrite and primary ferrite were identified. In this study, the influence of temperature on the crack propagation of as-cast AHSS was investigated. The temperatures chosen were from 200 °C to 600 °C, which is within the low cracking temperature range reported by industry for AHSS slabs. Since the different microstructures and various chemical compositions can affect mechanical behavior, this study examined whether the microstructures and chemical compositions influence how and why these steels crack over a range of temperatures.

sections.heading: Materials
paragraphs: Laboratory-cast ingots are used in this study, with the compositions (in wt pct) given in Table  I  (main elements) and the remaining elements in Table  II . A schematic of ingot sectioning is illustrated in both Figures  1 (a) and (b). Fig. 1 Schematic of ingot dimensions (left) and slab cut showing individual slabs sectioned into five sections (A through E) in which the tensile samples were taken from the A, B, D, and E sections (right)

Threaded round tensile specimens were cut and machined from the ingots using sections A, B, D, and E (schematic shown in Figure  1 ). The samples were round-threaded 10-mm tensile bar specimens with a reduced central section of 6 mm diameter by 6 mm length (Figure  2 ). This specific sample geometry was chosen to ensure a uniform temperature region in the hot zone of the sample during resistive heating. Fig. 2 The schematic of a Gleeble specimen showing a round-threaded 10-mm end tensile bar with a reduced central section of 6 mm diameter by 6 mm length

sections.heading: Hardness testing and predicted ferrite hardness calculation
paragraphs: Vickers hardness testing was performed on the Wilson VH3100 Hardness tester using 0.1 kgf load on each sample. Approximately 20 to 30 indentations were collected for each sample at different locations for different types of microstructures. The spacings between each indentation were 0.5 mm both in the horizontal and vertical direction and the ferrite is three times wider than each indentation to ensure valid measurements. For each composition, at least 100 indentations were made for each composition on samples taken from the center and edge of the ingots to test whether there is variability in hardness across the ingots.

sections.heading: 200 °C to 600 °C tensile testing
paragraphs: All samples were tested using a Gleeble 3500-GTC. A K-type thermocouple with diameter of 0.2 mm was spot-welded to the center of the reduced center section of each sample to monitor the temperature during the tests. The grips used for all tests were stainless steel. All tests were performed using a strain rate of 0.1 mm/s. Three testing temperatures were selected (200 °C, 400 °C, and 600 °C), spanning the low-temperature cracking region reported for AHSS slabs in industry and remaining below the lower end of the expected ductility dip (around 700 °C). At least three tests were carried out per temperature per composition.

sections.heading: Characterization methods
paragraphs: The reduction in area of each fractured specimen was measured with a caliper for all compositions at all tested temperatures. All fractured tensile samples were imaged, using various SEMs (Quanta 600, TESCAN Mira 3 FEG SEM and Phenom Particle X). Void lengths were measured for all compositions at all tested temperatures. Both the major and minor axes were measured since the majority of voids appeared ellipsoidal.

sections.heading: Fracture path observation
paragraphs: After all tensile tests, each sample was cut using a low-speed saw, and the fracture surfaces were reassembled and cross sectioned to view the fracture path. A schematic of how this was done is shown in Figure  3 . All samples were mechanically polished down to 1  μ m and the samples were etched with 5 pct nital followed by 1.3 pct aqueous picric acid. All samples were then imaged and characterized using the light optical microscope Zeiss Axio Imager.Z2 Vario. Fig. 3 Schematic of a fractured specimen reassembled for cross-section imaging

After being reassembled, the fractured specimens were imaged optically to determine if the crack propagates along the ferrite films. This quantification was done by measuring the ferrite line fraction along both sides of the fracture (Figure  4 ). Fig. 4 Example illustration showing how the ferrite was measured and quantified for a steel sample in pixel values showing ( a ) 3 Mn 1.5 Si 1.5 Al, which have a large ferrite percentage and ( b ) 3 Mn 1 Si 1 Al, which have a small ferrite percentage

The measured line fractions of ferrite along the crack path were averaged based on 10 to 15 measurements per temperature per composition and compared against the bulk (average ingot) ferrite percentage to determine whether the sample preferentially cracked along the ferrite films.

sections.heading: Hardness Results
paragraphs: Vickers hardness results are summarized in Figure  5 . Fig. 5 Average ingot, ferrite, and bainite Vickers Hardness with their respective uncertainties (95 pct confidence interval on the mean) for all compositions grouped according to total Al + Si concentrations of 1, 2, and 3 pct
A summary of the volume fraction and morphology of ferrite for all compositions is as shown in Table  III .

The hardness of Si-alloyed steels (without Al) is highest among all other compositions with 3 Si being the hardest steel. For 1 wt pct total addition steels, the ferrite percent is lower or not apparent under the hardness tester and so no ferrite hardness was recorded. For the 2 wt pct total addition group, there is a decrease in the hardness as Al increases for both bainite and ferrite as 2 Si has the highest bainite, ferrite, and average hardness compared against all three steels. For the 3 wt pct total addition group, as Al increases, the hardness decreases for both the bainite and the average ingot, while the ferrite plateaus at around 230 HV for the Al + Si steels.

sections.heading: Tensile Results
paragraphs: The force  vs  displacement curves from the tensile results are summarized in Figure  6 . In general, the yield strengths approximated from the force–displacement curves generated from the Gleeble are highest at 400 °C for most compositions, and the ductility is higher at 400 °C and 600 °C than at 200 °C. At 600 °C, most compositions have similar ductility and yield strengths regardless of the Si and Al additions. Fig. 6 Force (kN)  vs  displacement (mm) diagram for all compositions based on total addition: ( a ) 1 wt pct, ( b ) 2 wt pct, and ( c ) 3 wt pct at 200 °C, 400 °C, and 600 °C

The yield strengths for all compositions were approximated by identifying the yield point prior to the deviation from linearity observed in the force-displacement curves (shown in Figure  6 ). This point is identified as the force at yield. To obtain the yield strength, this force is divided by the cross-sectional area of the reduced center section. The approximate yield strengths for all compositions are summarized in Figure  7 . Fig. 7 Approximate yield strength (MPa) for all compositions at ( a ) 200 °C, ( b ) 400 °C, and ( c ) 600 °C grouped according to their total Al + Si additions of left: 1 wt pct, middle: 2 wt pct, and right: 3 wt pct

SEM images of the fracture surfaces taken for all samples tested at temperatures 200 °C, 400 °C, and 600 °C are shown in Figure  8 . Fig. 8 SEM images for the fracture surfaces of all compositions showing from left to right ( a ) 1 Si, 0.5 Si 0.5 Al and 1 Al with the labeled fracture characteristics; ( b ) 2 Si, 1 Si 1 Al and 2 Al, and ( c ) 3 Si, 2 Si 1 Al, 1.5 Si 1.5 Al and 1 Si 2 Al at temperatures 200 °C, 400 °C, and 600 °C

From the failed Gleeble samples, the reduction in area was measured for all compositions and is summarized in Figure  9  for all tested temperatures. From the SEM images (as shown in Figure  8 ), the predominant type of fracture for all compositions at various temperatures was also determined and is indicated through the different markers as shown in Fig.  9 . Fig. 9 Reduction in area measurements for Al + Si additions of ( a ) 1 wt pct, ( b ) 2 wt pct, ( c ) 3 wt pct at temperatures 200 °C, 400 °C, and 600 °C, where the different alloy total additions are indicated with different marker colors (1 wt pct: black, 2 wt pct blue, 3 wt pct: red) and the predominant fracture types are illustrated with different markers (Color figure online)

All compositions but 0.5 Si 0.5 Al have some ductility, where bimodal voids were observed. To understand the difference in the fracture surfaces in 0.5 Si 0.5 Al, SEM images for the 1 Si and 0.5 Si 0.5 Al steels are compared. At each temperature, one low-magnification image and one higher-magnification image are shown for each composition (Figure  10 ).

The trend between the measured void lengths and ductility is shown in Figure  11 . Fig. 11 Reduction in area (pct)  vs  void lengths ( μ m) for all compositions based on total addition: ( a ) 1 wt pct, ( b ) 2 wt pct and ( c ) 3 wt pct with voids observed from the SEM images. The graphs show both minor and major void lengths at the three tested temperatures

sections.heading: Fracture Path Observations
paragraphs: After the fracture surfaces were observed for all samples, failed Gleeble samples were reassembled and cut to observe the fracture path and investigate if the fracture follows along the ferrite. Optical images for all samples containing ferrite are shown in Figure  12 . Fig. 12 Optical images of fractured samples for all samples tested at temperatures of 200 °C, 400 °C, and 600 °C for ( a ) 2 wt pct total Si + Al addition and ( b ) 3 wt pct total Si + Al addition, where white microstructures are ferrite (as labeled in the figure). Optical images of fractured samples for all samples tested at temperatures of 200 °C, 400 °C, and 600 °C

From the optical images, the ferrite percentages on the fracture path were quantified. The ferrite percentages are summarized in Figure  13 . Fig. 13 Ferrite (pct) on the cracked path against all test temperatures of 200 °C, 400 °C, and 600 °C for ( a ) 2 wt pct total Al + Si and ( b ) 3 wt pct total Al + Si. Graph indicates the average bulk ferrite (shown as line) and average ferrite on the cracked path (shown as individual points)

sections.heading: Hardness Testing
paragraphs: Hardness results at room temperature indicated that hardness is highest for individual Si-alloyed steels and hardness increased with increasing Si addition. It is observed that 3 pct Si (3 pct Mn) has the highest hardness overall with highest bainite and ferrite hardness. This can in part be explained by the addition of Si enhancing the solid-solution strengthening effect. [ 13 ]  For the 1 wt pct Al + Si (3 Mn) and 2 wt pct Al + Si (3 Mn) groups, hardness decreases linearly with increasing Al addition for all ingot, ferrite, and bainite hardnesses. This could be due to the increasing amounts of ferrite observed in the Al-alloyed steels, and the weaker solid-solution strengthening effect of Al (compared with Si). For the 3 wt pct total (Al + Si) group, the trend remains the same for both average ingot and bainite hardnesses with the exception of ferrite where it remains within the same range.

With these calculations, the results are as shown in Figure  14 , where a linear fit and the  R 2  value are shown. Fig. 14 Calculated ferrite hardness values with the addition of intrinsic strength of iron and Hall–Petch ferrite grain calculations (HV predicted )  vs  actual hardness values (HV actual ) for all compositions with ferrite percentage indicated next to each marker points. A linear fit for the values is as shown in the figure. The legend indicates the different ferrite morphologies identified for each steel composition (as shown previously in Table  III ) and the  R 2  value from the linear fit

From this comparison, the hardness of the primary ferrite group seems to be overpredicted, while that of the proeutectoid ferrite group is underpredicted. The  R 2  value from the linear fitting also showed that the fitting is poor which indicates the model used is not valid for the current compositions. This could be attributed to the highly alloyed steel, where Mn, Si, and Al all influence the ferrite hardness. Hence, Leslie’s model is only considered in this case as a preliminary comparison with the ferrite hardnesses observed experimentally, where the observed values are considered as within the range and reasonable to the calculated ones (Figure  15 ). Fig. 15 Calculated hardness contributions for solid-solution strengthening, intrinsic strength, and Hall–Petch ferrite grain strength

The hardness contributions indicated that the Hall–Petch ferrite grain strength contributed the most to the predicted ferrite strength of the alloys followed by solid-solution strengthening and intrinsic strength. Overall, individual Al steels such as 2 Al have the lowest ferrite hardness followed by Si + Al addition steels and 3 Si having the highest ferrite hardness.

sections.heading: Tensile Results
paragraphs: From previous microstructural investigation, [ 2 ]  bainite and ferrite were present for most steel with 3 Mn 1 Al having only bainite in the microstructure. While the ferrite volume fraction increases with increasing Si, Al, and Si + Al addition, the trend is persistent for all steels. With two ferrite types previously identified, proeutectoid ferrite and primary ferrite, it is predicted that the microstructural difference will affect the yield strengths and ductility of the steels. Apart from the microstructural differences, another factor that can also affect the mechanical properties of the steels is microsegregation. Microsegregation is present for all compositions except for the ones with primary ferrite (Al and Si + Al steels), which can be observed from the optical images. While macrosegregation is a potential cause for slab cracking, it is not observed in the laboratory cast ingots in this study and hence will not be considered as a factor for cracking.

From the force–displacement curves shown for all compositions, the individual Si-alloyed steels in general have higher yield strengths at 200 °C and 400 °C compared to the other compositions, where Si with Al compositions have lower yield strengths. The quantification of this is observed in Figure  7 , where the approximated yield strengths are taken for all compositions. The graph indicates that as the total alloy concentration increases, the approximate yield strength also increases at all three tested temperatures.

Comparing all three tested temperatures, all compositions have the lowest yield strength at 600 °C, while most had highest yield strengths at 400 °C. It is suspected that 400 °C is the intermediate temperature, where the tendency of carbon to pin dislocations increases which raises the yield strength of the alloys. [ 27 ]  Around this temperature, it is also reported that the clinking phenomenon occurs. [ 28 ]  Fracture toughness values found around this temperature range were rather low [ 28 ]  and since it is known that toughness and yield strengths have an inverse relationship, it is suggested that these steels could undergo clinking at this temperature. Clinking is a phenomenon that occurs where slabs crack upon cooling after continuous casting and before going into the reheat furnace. [ 28 ]  Since it is a catastrophic phenomenon that happens around the lower temperatures, it is crucial to this work as the cracking mechanisms such as grain size identified in this work are some factors that could impact this crack behavior. However, without knowing the stress or strain localization in the steel, this is only a prediction and should be validated with further experiments.

Steels with higher Si (and no added Al) showed a clear increase in yield strength (with increased Si). By partially replacing the Si in the steel with Al, it is seen that the yield strength is much lower compared to the Si-only alloyed steels. The highest yield strength for Si + Al steels is observed in 3 Mn 1 Si 1 Al, which has a comparable strength to the 1 Si steel at all three tested temperatures. For Si + Al-alloyed steels with a higher total addition (3 wt pct instead of 2 wt pct), the yield strength is lower.

It is found that for steels with both Si and Al additions, the ones with a lower Si to Al ratio have higher yield strength and elongation compared to the ones with a higher Si-to-Al ratio. [ 29 ]  In the current work, when comparing steels with different Si to Al ratios and the same total Si + Al addition—3 Mn 1 Si 2 Al and 3 Mn 2 Si 1 Al—it is observed that the steel with the higher Si to Al ratio has a slightly higher yield strength than for the lower Si-to-Al ratio, contrary to the literature observation. However, the literature values are for processed AHSS, not as-cast ingots as studied here. A possible reason why the findings contradict the literature could be due to the microstructure where ferrite amounts are higher in 3 Mn 2 Si 1 Al, with the increase in ferrite leading to a lower the yield strength.

For individual Al-alloyed steels, the yield strength is much lower when compared to individual Si-alloyed steels, but the values are similar to the Si + Al steels. This is expected as literature [ 30 ]  pointed out that the under similar strain rates, the Si steels will have higher strengths than Al steels. However, detailed comparisons show that several high total additions (≥ 2 wt pct) Si + Al steels show higher yield strength than individual Al steels.

The ductility of different compositions was also compared. For 1 wt pct total addition, the 1 Al steel is most ductile across all temperatures. Similarly, 1 Si 1 Al is more ductile than 2 Si across all temperatures for 2 wt pct total addition. For 3 wt pct, all three Si + Al alloys have similar ductility and yield strengths with 3 Si have the lowest ductility.

To understand factors that can influence the ductility apart from temperature, void lengths were measured and compared against the reduction in area for all compositions (with the exception of 0.5 Si 0.5 Al, where no voids were observed). As the test temperature increased, the reduction in area and the void lengths increased linearly for most compositions. While there are some cases where the increase is unclear, void lengths were largest at 600 °C when compared to 200 °C. There seems to be some overlap at the lower temperatures (200 °C and 400 °C) and in some compositions both temperatures gave similar ductility and void lengths. Since higher temperatures mean that there are fewer nucleating particles, larger void sizes can enhance the ductility of the steel. [ 31 ]  The major and minor void lengths are similar for all cases.

Observing the fracture surfaces for all compositions at the three tested temperatures, ductile fracture with the presence of dimples, microvoids and bimodal voids were most commonly seen. At 200 °C, the fracture surfaces vary as all individual Si-alloyed steels contain both brittle and ductile fracture, with both cleavage and voids. At higher temperatures, all individual Si-alloyed steels show primarily ductile fracture. For all individual Al-alloyed and Si + Al steels (except 0.5 Si 0.5 Al), ductile fracture was observed at all three tested temperatures. In several cases, shear fracture was discovered in certain regions, where no voids were present across a fracture surface and in other cases ripple lines were present.

Across all steel compositions, 3 Mn 0.5 Si 0.5 Al is the only exception, where brittle fracture was noticed for all three tested temperatures. Since 0.5 Si 0.5 Al and 1 Si have similar total Al + Si additions (1 wt pct) and both show intergranular cracking, they were compared in more detail. From both the high- and low-magnification SEM images, some microvoids were seen for 1 Si even at 200 °C, while none was observed for 0.5 Si 0.5 Al. The morphology of the fracture surfaces in 0.5 Si 0.5 Al was also different from the rest of the brittle fractures observed. While it is not apparent from the low-magnification images [Figure  10 (b)], each grain surface showed a different fracture morphology.

For the intergranular cracking behavior observed throughout all three temperatures, it is hypothesized that the behavior is related to AlN (aluminum nitride) precipitates existing along the prior austenite grain boundaries (PAGBs). According to Wilson and Gladman, for the as-cast steels with low cooling rates (below 1 °C/min), the AlN morphologies can either be (1) large and thin dendrites (less than 10 nm) that form from solute later in the solidification step or (2) plate-like (with thicknesses up to 65 nm) that nucleated on the PAGBs and grow as thin plates with respect to the grain orientation. [ 32 ]

The “rock candy” fracture seen could possibly be caused by the existence of dendritic and plate-like AlN at the PAGBs. It is found that any AlN present within a strong matrix can cause failure to occur preferentially along the PAGBs resulting in a rock-candy fracture seen from the SEM images. [ 33 ]  The increase in intergranular fracture due to AlN precipitates can cause a great decrease in the impact strength. [ 33 ]  Nevertheless, the rock-candy fracture does not necessarily lead to a decrease in the tensile or yield strength but can greatly impact the materials’ properties depending on temperature and strain rates. [ 34 ]  This agrees with the yield strength results (Figures  6  and  7 ), where 0.5 Si 0.5 Al appeared to have the lowest yield strengths at all temperatures when compared with other compositions either within 1 wt pct addition group or higher. Attempts were made to observe if any AlN inclusions were present on the PAGBs yet only one case of AlN was observed under SEM. To confirm the presence of AlN on the PAGBs, it is recommended to utilize TEM analysis for more accurate observations.

Due to the brittle failure at and below 600 °C, it is not recommended to cast 3 Mn 0.5 Si 0.5 Al as current tensile results indicate that the slabs may crack if left to cool after continuous casting. With the brittle nature of this steel, it is likely that the surface and edges of the slab will crack first which can then propagate through the entire slab. Given this insight, it is recommended to potentially alter the Si and Al addition as ductile failure is observed as the Si and Al addition increases as can be seen in the 3 Mn 1 Si 1 Al case.

With the fracture surfaces identified and reductions in area measured for all compositions, several trends were noted. There are four common fracture surfaces identified: brittle, brittle and ductile, ductile (including shear fracture), and all where all includes brittle, ductile, and shear fracture. Specimens with brittle fracture had a lower reduction in area than those with little or no brittle fracture. This applies to 0.5 Si 0.5 Al as brittle fracture was observed for all three temperatures. Regardless, as the tested temperature increases, the reduction in area increases. Both compositions—3 Mn 1 Si 1 Al and 3 Mn 1.5 Si 1.5 Al—have the highest recorded reduction in area reaching almost 50 pct at 600 °C.

With the current findings, several problems could be identified that may eventually lead to slab clinking. One fracture problem identified for individual Si-alloyed steels and 3 Mn 0.5 Si 0.5 Al is intergranular fracture due to large-sized grains crack (approximately 500 to 3000  μ m). Another problem identified is brittle failure at temperatures at or lower than 400 °C for the individual Si-alloyed and low Si + Al steels. Brittle failure can potentially cause slab fracture and if combined with the large grain sizes, it could be a catastrophic failure as cracks can propagate through the entire slab. Several suggestions could be made to help mitigate clinking to cause in slabs. One suggestion is to use compositions that have high ductility at the lower temperatures (≤ 400 °C) to prevent brittle failure as the slabs cool after continuous casting. Compositions that have shown to have higher ductility at the lower temperatures include 2 Al, 1 Si 1 Al and 1.5 Si 1.5 Al, where the average ductility is around 20 pct at 400 °C. Another suggestion is to hot charge the slabs for compositions with known large grain sizes and brittle failure. Without hot charging, it would be problematic to leave the slabs to cool down before being processed and it is recommended to study the hot charging temperature as it may differ between compositions depending on the Si and Al additions in the steel.

sections.heading: Fracture Path Observations
paragraphs: To determine where the ferrite influences the crack path, ferrite quantification was done. If ferrite measured along the crack path is higher than the average bulk ferrite, the steels crack preferentially along the ferrite path. If the measured ferrite along the crack path is lower than the bulk ferrite, the steels do not crack preferentially along the ferrite path.

From the ferrite quantification shown, it showed that the ferrite percentages along the ferrite crack path are mostly lower than the bulk ferrite measured for most compositions. While there were some instances, where the measured ferrite is higher than the bulk ferrite, these values typically fall within the uncertainty range of the bulk ferrite. Hence, for all compositions, the crack does not propagate along the ferrite for all compositions. This finding contrasts with the previous Charpy results, [ 22 ]  where the crack propagated along the ferrite films. The difference in these results is not caused by differences in the characterization method: the previous results, on similar as-cast steel compositions, were also obtained by optical microscopy of fracture surfaces. The stress state and deformation rate were quite different, though, in the current work, tensile tests were performed—giving no preferential failure through the ferrite—whereas the previous work used impact tests, with rapid failure and triaxial stress at the notch, and failure through ferrite.

While ferrite may not be the primary influence for the crack to occur, there are various factors that influence cracking in the microstructure. A previous study by Basantia  et al . [ 35 ]  on the effects of microstructures on mechanical properties for ferrite–bainite, ferrite–martensite, and ferrite–pearlite steels showed that the hard microstructural constituents such as bainite, martensite, and pearlite have significantly higher stresses than ferrite. The difference in the stresses among the different phases is attributed to the difference in the hardness values. At the interface of hard bainite and soft ferrite, microvoids are observed which eventually would coalesce and propagate along the ferrite films.

Another study on ferrite–bainite DP steel by Kumar  et al . [ 36 ]  indicated that the crack path is dependent on the volume fraction of bainite and the bainite strength variation, which is dependent on the carbon partitioning. For the steel with 82.5 pct bainite, it is observed that the bainite–bainite interface is the preferential crack path and is believed to have been influenced by the phosphorus (P) segregation due to the 0.017 wt pct P in the steel. It is mentioned that P can lower the intergranular fracture energy at the bainite–bainite interface, which influences the crack path of the steel. Considering the steels used in this study has approximately 0.015 wt pct P, it is highly probable that the crack path follows the bainite–bainite interface, which explains the low probability of the steels cracking along the ferrite films.

It was mentioned previously that microsegregation could be a potential cause for cracking in these steels. With the P segregation along the bainite–bainite interface, [ 36 ]  it is possible that the microsegregation of minor elements may affect the cracking propagation of these steels. However, from the fractured optical images (in Figure  12 ), the crack path did not seem to follow any observable microsegregation paths. Hence, it could only be concluded in this study that the crack path may possibly follow along the segregated P regions in the bainite–bainite interface and further investigation is needed to confirm this potential cause.

sections.heading: Alloy Addition Comparisons
paragraphs: With the previous paper [ 2 ]  investigating the microstructural differences of Si, Al, and Si + Al steels, the current results add to the understanding of alloy composition effects on the steel microstructures and properties. It is found that replacing Si with Al either partially or entirely can increase the ferrite fraction, which can decrease alloy hardness. Comparing the individual Si-alloyed steels to individual Al-alloyed or Si + Al combined steels, the average hardness of individual Si-alloyed steel is highest.

Similarly, individual Si-alloyed steels have higher yield strengths than the individual Al-alloyed or combined Si + Al steels. While some of the combined Si + Al steels have comparable strength to the lower addition individual Si-alloyed steels, others fall within the same range and are lower at lower testing temperatures (200 °C and 400 °C). In terms of ductility, replacing Si with Al partially increases ductility at all three tested temperatures, while individual Si-alloyed steels and individual Al-alloyed steels show similar ductility. There is no difference among the varying chemical compositions and the cracking behavior, which propose a different cracking mechanism that the steels could experience.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This paper explored the mechanical properties of various alloyed as-cast AHSS. With the motivation of investigating why the AHSS slabs crack at temperatures below 400 °C, several conclusions can be drawn: Room-temperature Vickers hardness testing indicates that individual Si-alloyed steels (specifically 3 Si) have the highest hardness followed by high addition Si + Al steels with individual Al-alloyed steels having the lowest hardness. Highest recorded yield strengths are for individual Si-alloyed steels and 1 Si 1 Al, where the yield strengths are about 1 GPa and above at 200 °C and 400 °C. For the remaining compositions, the yield strengths are comparable as the testing temperature increases to 600 °C. For compositions with higher yield strengths, their reduction in area is generally lower except for 1 Si 1 Al, where the reduction in area reached 20 pct at 400 °C, which is comparable to other compositions which have lower strength. Three common fracture types were identified among all compositions: brittle, mixed (brittle and ductile), and ductile fracture; ductile fracture is most common for all compositions with the exception of 0.5 Si 0.5 Al, which cracked in a brittle manner at all testing temperatures, and individual Si-alloyed steels (combined brittle and ductile failure at 200 °C). There is no indication that the fracture path follows the ferrite films indicating that there could be other factors such as segregation of P along the bainite–bainite interface that can influence the crack path. A possible effect of both the higher flow stress and triaxial stress during impact testing is to promote the nucleation of voids within ferrite, leading to ductile tearing through ferrite. Additional impact testing on the as-cast steels would be needed to evaluate whether this effect holds across the range of microstructures encountered in the current work.
